questions.stem: What did the librarian question in A1?
options: Whether more books alone would improve access
Whether the library should stop lending
questions.explanation: A1 distinguishes a larger collection from residents being able to reach it. The other options are not stated.
questions.passage:
[A1] A district library wanted more residents to use its collection. Its first proposal was to buy several thousand new books. That sounded sensible: a larger collection might offer something for everyone. Yet a librarian asked the team to examine a less visible problem. A person who could not reach the building during opening hours would gain little from an extra shelf of books.
[A2] The team spoke with residents at a bus stop, a market and a workplace canteen. These conversations were not a representative survey, and the team did not present them as one. They did, however, reveal situations worth investigating. Some residents worked when the library was open. Others could reach the building but found the registration instructions difficult. A few did not know that membership was free. The common problem was not simply a shortage of books.
[A3] Rather than abandon its collection plan, the library tried a limited change. For eight weeks, it opened two hours later on one evening and used a shorter registration form. Staff wrote down attendance by hour and invited anonymous comments. Evening visits increased. Several comments mentioned that the new time allowed people to come after work. The records did not show whether the same visitors had merely changed their visiting time, however, so the team could not calculate the number of entirely new users.
[A4] The trial also had costs. Later opening required a different staff schedule, and an employee pointed out that a bus service ended before the building closed. Keeping the doors open was not enough if some residents could no longer travel home. The team therefore checked transport times before deciding on a permanent timetable. It also kept paper forms for residents who preferred not to register online.
[A5] At the next budget meeting, the director described access and collection quality as connected goals, not competing slogans. Better books remained useful, but their value depended partly on whether people could actually use them. The team had not found a single solution for all residents. It had learned to ask whose difficulty a change addressed, what evidence supported it and what new difficulty it might create.

options: Fluency is not the same as factual correctness
A quick reply must be correct
questions.explanation: C1 contrasts well-written wording with wrong order information.
questions.passage:
[C1] A small publishing office tested software that suggested replies to common customer questions. The manager hoped it would save staff time. During the first demonstration, the software produced fluent sentences almost immediately. Several employees were impressed. One editor, however, noted that a reply could be well written and still give the wrong information about a particular order.
[C2] The office began with a narrow task. The tool could draft responses about opening hours and general delivery procedures, using a set of documents that staff had checked. It could not approve refunds, change an address or access private payment details. These restrictions made the trial less exciting to some observers, but the editor argued that a clear boundary was more useful than a vague promise of intelligence.
[C3] Staff reviewed every proposed reply before sending it. They recorded the question category, whether a suggestion needed correction and the time spent on review. They did not enter customer names into the trial log. In one category, the software often repeated an outdated instruction. The team corrected the source document and tested the same kind of question again. Better wording alone would not have fixed the underlying information problem.
[C4] At the end of the trial, simple questions usually took less time to answer, including review. Complex cases sometimes took longer because staff had to recognise what was missing and write a new response. The manager therefore reported results separately for the two categories. Combining all questions into one attractive average could have hidden a cost that mattered to the people doing the work. The trial also provided no evidence that similar software would perform equally well in a different organisation.
[C5] The office kept the tool for its limited purpose. Training sessions taught employees how to question a suggestion rather than accept it because it sounded confident. The editor described the aim as informed assistance: a system should make a human task easier without concealing the reasons for human judgment. For the office, the decision to use software remained a decision about responsibilities, information quality and actual working conditions, not a contest to remove people from every step.

questions.stem: How did the new project differ from previous exhibitions?
options: Students helped before the labels were finalised
Curators accepted every story as fact
questions.explanation: D1 says students were involved earlier rather than invited after selection and labelling.
questions.passage:
[D1] A local museum invited a school class to help design an exhibition about everyday life. In previous years, curators had selected objects and written labels before asking students to visit. This time, students were involved earlier. They brought photographs of ordinary items and explained why those items mattered to their families. A cooking pot and a bus ticket led to conversations that an expensive painting might not have started.
[D2] The curators did not accept every proposed story as established history. They asked students to distinguish what a family member remembered from what a dated document could show. Memory could offer a valuable perspective, but the date of an event sometimes needed another source. The aim was not to embarrass families for remembering differently. It was to make the relationship between a claim and its evidence visible.
[D3] One group wanted to label a tool as “used in every home”. The students had found it in three households, all connected to the same workplace. After discussing the sample, they replaced the phrase with a narrower description. The new label was less dramatic, but it said more accurately what they knew. Another group disagreed about the meaning of a photograph. Instead of forcing a single confident explanation, the exhibition presented two interpretations and explained why the available evidence did not settle the question.
[D4] Practical decisions mattered as well. Labels had to be readable from a reasonable distance. Audio descriptions were offered, but printed versions remained available. Some students enjoyed recording their voices; others preferred checking dates or arranging images. The teacher did not treat one kind of contribution as the only sign of learning. Different tasks could develop different skills, and students were asked to describe what they had learned rather than simply count the objects they had handled.
[D5] After the exhibition opened, visitors added comments about what was clear and what was confusing. The students revised several labels. For the teacher, this was not a sign that the first version had been worthless. It showed that public work could improve through attention to its audience. The project did not turn every student into a historian, but it gave the class practice in asking questions, checking support and communicating uncertainty without giving up the attempt to explain.

questions.answer:
The chart shows a change in the ways members contacted a fictional community centre. Online enquiries rose from 40 to 70 per week, while telephone enquiries fell from 50 to 35. Visits to the desk changed only slightly, from 30 to 32. These figures describe the recorded contacts; they do not tell us how many different people used each route.
One possible explanation is that the centre made its website easier to use. However, the chart alone cannot establish this cause. Opening hours, publicity and changes in the people seeking help may also matter. It would therefore be unwise to close the telephone service simply because its recorded use declined. Some residents may depend on it even when the online total is higher.
The centre could ask users what difficulties they experience and compare the quality of responses across routes. A sensible decision would combine the counts with evidence about access and service needs. Progress should mean making useful help easier to obtain, not merely moving more activity onto a screen.
